list.listitem: Most patients with mild aphthae require no treatment or only periodic topical therapy (amlexanox, steroids, and tetracycline). B
There is no proven preventive therapy, although amlexanox may be beneficial if taken in the prodromal phase. Topic corticosteroids are recommended to reduce pain and duration of symptoms. C
Thalidomide reduces pain and duration of ulcers in severe cases in patients with HIV disease. B
Consider further testing in severe or recurrent disease with CBC, vitamin B12 and folate levels, iron, cultures, or biopsy if clinically indicated. B

background.definition: Aphthous ulcers are solitary or multiple painful ulcerations ("canker sores") that occur on the labial, buccal, lingual, sublingual, palatal, or gingival mucosa. Recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS) occurs in 50% of patients with aphthous ulcers. Three forms exist: (1) minor - solitary, smaller than 1 cm; (2) major - multiple or larger than 1 cm; and (3) herpetiform - multiple and vesicular in quality.

list.listitem: 10% (range 5%-25%), with 3-month recurrence rates as high as 50%.
The etiology of aphthous stomatitis is probably multifactorial.
It typically starts in childhood, with 50% of cases having a positive family history.
Studies are conflicting, but trauma, emotional stress, and food hypersensitivities have been implicated.
Hematologic deficiency is present in 20% of patients (iron, folic acid, and vitamin B12).
Smoking is associated with a lower prevalence of disease.
No infectious process has been identified as a cause of aphthous ulcers.
Antineoplastic drugs are associated with recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS).
There is an increased risk of RAS in persons with with polymorphism of IL-1β (+3954C/T) (OR, 1.5) and IL-1β (-511C/T) (OR, 1.4).
HIV-positive patients with a CD4 count of less than 100 U/mL are at increased risk.
In a small case-control study, aphthous ulcers were more frequent in patients with celiac disease than controls (42.4% vs. 23.2%, P = 0.02).
This was confirmed in a meta-analysis of 21 case-control studies that found a higher incidence of RAS in patients with celiac disease (25% vs 11%; OR, 3.8).

A condition called oral mucosal fixed drug eruption (FDE) has been reported; patients presented with solitary lesions predominantly on the dorsum of the tongue or hard palate and presented as bullae, aphthous or erythematous lesions. The primary implicated drugs were naproxen and cotrimoxazole.

Effectively eradicating H. pylori is associated with a significant increase in vitamin B12 levels and a significant decrease in the mean number of aphthous ulcers compared to patients without H. pylori eradication.
A significant association between COVID-19 and RAS has been reported. Feamles and younger patients are more likely to develop aphthous ulcers associated with COVID-19.,
The precise pathogenesis is unknown.
Aphthous ulcers are thought to be caused by an altered local regulation of the cell-mediated immune system.
Activation and accumulation of cytotoxic T cells lead to epithelial cell death, which may contribute to the localized mucosal breakdown.
No screening is necessary. C
Treating hematologic deficiencies may prevent recurrences. B
Use of elimination diets may prevent recurrences. B
Aphthous stomatitis is primarily a clinical diagnosis. C

Consider autoimmune disorders (Behçet's syndrome, celiac disease, Reiter's syndrome, Crohn's disease, systemic lupus erythematosus [SLE]) or immunocompromised states with severe or recurrent episodes. C
Consider hematologic deficiencies (vitamin B12, folate, and iron) if anemia is present or nutritional deficiency is suspected. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Vesicular, primarily on vermillion border, crusting in 24 to 48 hours
Children; hand, foot, and buttocks lesions

list.listitem: The typical patient presents with small, shallow, well-circumscribed round ulcers with an erythematous halo and a gray fibrinous exudate on the buccal, lingual, gingival, or palatal mucosa. A prodrome of pricking or burning may precede the lesions by 24 to 48 hours.
There are usually no associated signs of systemic illness such as fever, rash, or lymphadenopathy.

A syndrome characterized by periodic fever accompanied by aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis and cervical adenitis (PFAPA) has been identified. In 1 case series (N = 15), patients reported monthly episodes of fever at approximately 4 week intervals, beginning at a mean age of 20.9 years, with attacks recurring in later years at 4 to 8 week intervals. Patients were otherwise healthy. Oral prednisone in a single 60-mg dose aborted attacks in all patients.
Consider recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS) if ulcers occur at intervals of 1 to 4 months, or if less frequent but more severe episodes occur.
Suspect another diagnosis if lesions fail to heal within 14 days, if nonoral ulcers are present, if systemic signs or symptoms are present, or if the patient is in an immunocompromised state.

Other etiologies to consider in patients with an oral manifestation of a systemic disease include infectious (herpes simplex virus, HIV, fungal, etc.), autoimmune (Behçet's syndrome, Reiter's syndrome, SLE, bullous pemphigoid, etc.), or malignant (squamous cell carcinoma).
No diagnostic testing is indicated unless other diagnoses are suspected or when lesions last longer than 14 days.

Tests that may be helpful if clinically indicated include biopsy for a nonhealing ulcer, culture for lesions consistent with a fungal or bacterial infection, HIV test, and CBC with additional risk factors or patients in an immunocompromised state (eg, steroids, chemotherapy, etc.).
Order vitamin B12, folate, and iron tests if a deficiency is suspected based on a CBC or dietary history.
No relevant clinical decision rules found.
An aphthous ulcer is a clinical diagnosis based on the presence of typical lesions that heal in 7 to 14 days. RAS is diagnosed when lesions reoccur at 1- to 4-month intervals.

Other diagnoses should be considered when ulcers last longer than 14 days, when nonoral ulcers are present, when systemic signs or symptoms are present, or if the patient is in an immunocompromised state.
Amlexanox 5% oral paste is the only FDA-approved treatment. (A summary of treatments is given in .) B
Topical steroids are first-line treatment. B
Thalidomide may be used in severe and unresponsive cases. B
Amlexanox oral paste (Aphthasol) is effective in reducing pain and lesion size and is the only FDA-approved drug. Apply 1/4 in to lesion 4 times a day.
Amlexanox may aid in prevention of ulcers if used in the prodromal phase.
A review recommends topical corticosteroids as first-line therapy for recurrent aphthous stomatitis.
Viscous lidocaine will give temporary relief (use before eating).
Chlorhexidine mouth wash significantly increases the interval between successive ulcers.

Tetracycline (250-mg tablet dissolved in water or syrup 250 mg/5 mL; swish and spit 4 times daily for 4-5 days) reduces duration and pain but not frequency of ulcerations. Do not use in children younger than 9 years.

Topical corticosteroids reduce pain and duration but not frequency. Dexamethasone elixir: 0.5 mg/5 mL water; swish and spit 5 mL every 12 hours. Triamcinolone in Orabase: apply to dry ulcer 2 to 4 times a day until ulcer is healed.

Vitamin B12, iron, and folate deficiency are more common in patients with recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS); case reports and observational studies have shown an association between treatment for the hematologic deficiency and fewer recurrences.
In 1 study of patients without vitamin B12 deficiency, sublingual vitamin B12 (1000 mcg) significantly reduced the duration, number and subjective pain level of RAS.
Silver nitrate application decreased pain but not duration in one study.
In patients with severe RAS, consider oral corticosteroids (although based on case reports only).
Thalidomide is effective but use only in severe cases and in patients with HIV.
Probiotics decrease outbreak frequency within the 6 months after treatment in children but not in adults.
A Cochrane review of 25 trials (22 of which were placebo controlled) determined that there was insufficient evidence to support or refute any intervention.
Cryotherapy is ineffective.

A network meta-analyis that included 11 studies with laser interventions in recurrent aphthous stomatitis (RAS) revealed that laser therapy can be used as a short-term intervention during the exacerbation phase of ulcers to promote healing and reduce pain. .

Myrtle paste (applied 4 times daily for 6 days) was significantly more effective than placebo paste in decreasing the size of ulcers, pain severity and the level of erythema and exudation, and improving the quality of life in patients who suffer from RAS.
In a small RCT, an over-the-counter medicated intraoral adhesive patch containing extract of glycyrrhiza root was more effective than placebo patch or no treatment in pain reduction.
Use of an elimination diet for possible triggers (commonly wheat, barley, rye, oats, and cow's milk) has shown some benefit.
Amlexanox may aid in prevention of ulcers and decrease symptoms if used in the prodromal phase.

In a small clinical trial, oral polio vaccine, administered in a dose of 4 drops at monthly intervals for 3 months, was more effective than placebo in frequency and duration of ulcers in patients with RAS.
Dermatologic referral is indicated with severe, unresponsive disease.
Aphthous ulcers are self-limited, and there are no permanent sequelae. C
Recurrence rates are high (50%). C
Be cautious and consider alternative diagnoses if RAS begins in the elderly.
In particular, rule out squamous cell carcinoma, an immunocompromised state from an occult malignancy, or nutritional deficiencies.
Avoid tetracycline therapy.
Amlexanox 5% is a pregnancy category B drug.
Avoid tetracycline therapy in children younger than 9 years.
